justification: A committed provision is inserted with v2_precinct_id UNSET. Nothing set it. Measured against production 2026-09-10: ashfield served 2,041 provisions with 118 keyed, marrickville 2,403 with 37, ku_ring_gai 337 with 0. The precincts had not changed -- the keys had been wiped by a re-extraction, exactly as derive_precinct_keys' own docstring predicts ('applied to rows BY HAND, so every re-extraction nulled them and the manual work recurred'). The July fix made the keys DERIVABLE but wired nothing to derive them: a repo-wide search of every .yml/.toml/.py/.json/.sh outside .claude/worktrees found no pipeline, cron or CI step that calls it. The user-visible effect is silent and wrong-shaped: a precinct lookup for an affected council returns council-wide controls instead of the precinct's own, with no error anywhere. This is the same failure class as DQ-30 (a one-time data cleanup with nothing guarding the write path that keeps re-breaking it).

falsifiable_check.command: python -m pytest tests/test_dcp_commit_rederives_precinct_keys.py tests/test_dockerfile_monitors_imports.py -q, then re-run against twelve separate reversions of the fix (block deleted; council=None bulk call; apply=False; validate=True; dry_run guard dropped; failed commits counted as committed; per-council try/except removed; warning no longer names the fixing command; narrow `except ImportError` instead of `except Exception`; warning no longer names the missing json; the json COPY removed from Dockerfile.monitors; the module COPY removed). Real layer, opt-in: PYTEST_REAL_DB=1 DATABASE_URL=... pytest -m database tests/test_dcp_commit_approved_real_db.py -o addopts="" (4 tests; skips cleanly to 4 skipped without the flag), forced red three ways: hide a RULES council from the provisions vocabulary, make --validate report a mismatch against the human-applied keys, rename a run() keyword.
falsifiable_check.fails_when: Any reversion leaves the suite green. The two that matter most are not the obvious ones. (1) A BULK call -- derive_precinct_keys.run() deliberately refuses validate:False rules unless a council is named, so `council=None` prints a tidy success total and silently leaves Ashfield's 641 chapter-D rows unkeyed; the scoping is load-bearing, not tidiness. (2) A NARROW `except ImportError` -- derive_precinct_keys open()s data/cos_precinct_page_ranges.json at MODULE level, so a packaging slip raises FileNotFoundError, which an ImportError handler does not catch, turning a run whose provisions are already committed and live into a crashed job. None of these is a self-comparison: the mutants are reversions that must go RED, and the independent authority is test_precinct_ancestor_resolution.py, which predates this branch, is untouched by it, and queries the live database directly.
falsifiable_check.observed_red: 11 of 12 reversions went red on the first pass; the 12th ('dry_run guard dropped') SURVIVED and was investigated rather than papered over. It survives because committed_councils is only populated in the non-dry-run branch, so `not dry_run` is currently redundant. A second mutation run proved the guard still earns its place: with a plausible refactor that records the council in the dry-run branch too, 'refactor only (guard present)' = 9 passed and 'refactor + guard removed' = 1 failed, so the dry-run test does catch its removal once the redundancy is gone. Separately, one assertion was found WEAK by mutation and fixed: the test's own FileNotFoundError message contained 'cos_precinct_page_ranges.json', so the assertion that the WARNING names the file was being satisfied by the exception text; the fake now raises a generic FileNotFoundError(2, 'No such file or directory') and that mutant is killed. Final: 4/4 on the packaging+import set, 7/8 on the wiring set with the 8th shown defended. Full suite after the fix: 5,182 passed, 2 skipped, 0 failed in 95s. Real-layer set: 3/3 mutants killed (1 failed, 3 passed each), and the file skips to '4 skipped in 0.23s' with no opt-in, so it cannot pass on a stubbed psycopg2. Against production it is 4 passed in 4.99s. Return-value set added after cross-review: 4/4 killed (return ignored; `continue` dropped so rc reads unbound/stale; success warns too, making the warning noise; warning loses the per-council command). Full suite after: 5,184 passed, 2 skipped, 0 failed in 85s.
falsifiable_check.real_data_check: The derivation this wires in was executed against production during the session that found the bug: bulk --apply wrote 887 keys, then --council ku_ring_gai --apply wrote 32 and --council ashfield --apply wrote 641, each with a rollback CSV. Result measured after: ashfield 118 -> 733 keyed, marrickville 37 -> 785, ku_ring_gai 0 -> 31, and tests/test_precinct_ancestor_resolution.py went from '2 failed, 9 passed' to '11 passed' against the real database. The script's own --validate pass ('every derived key on a validate-rule reproduces the existing key') passed before any write. The real-layer file now pins that agreement permanently rather than as a one-off session check: RULES councils and dcp_review_queue councils must both be subsets of regulatory_provisions.source_council, and derive_precinct_keys --validate must still return 0 against production.
falsifiable_check.external_authority: WHY THIS IS NOT SELF-REFERENTIAL, stated explicitly because part of it looks it. Three independent authorities, none of them this change's own output. (1) THE PRIMARY ONE: tests/test_precinct_ancestor_resolution.py, written 2026-08-20 for #990/#992, months before this branch, by a different piece of work, and NOT modified here. It asserts against the live database that ashfield 'Part 1' and marrickville '47_' resolve to served provisions. It went from '2 failed, 9 passed' to '11 passed' when the keys were restored. That test does not know this fix exists and cannot be satisfied by the derivation agreeing with itself. (2) HUMAN-APPLIED GROUND TRUTH: the keys --validate reproduces were applied BY HAND, row by row, before derive_precinct_keys existed -- that is the whole reason the script was written (its docstring: keys 'were applied to rows BY HAND'). So --validate compares a written rule against a human's independent judgement of which precinct a provision belongs to; it is a rule-vs-human comparison, not code re-running and agreeing with itself. It is also the weaker of the three and is not relied on alone. (3) FORCED FAILURE, not re-running: the 12 wiring/packaging mutants and the 3 real-layer mutants are reversions of the fix that must turn the suite red. A test that cannot fail proves nothing, so each was made to fail before being trusted -- including one assertion that mutation exposed as WEAK (it was being satisfied by the test's own exception text) and which was fixed rather than explained away.

pre_impl.existing_data: regulatory_provisions columns the derivation reads (id, document_id, ref_number, pdf_page, source_chapter_key, v2_precinct_id, v2_dcp_layer, v2_dcp_part, provision_text) were all confirmed live, and run() was executed successfully against production this session rather than inspected.
pre_impl.assumption_mismatch: Checked the council-slug vocabulary across all three systems, because a mismatch would make the scoped call silently no-op. (RULES councils - regulatory_provisions.source_council) is EMPTY and (dcp_review_queue.council - source_council) is EMPTY, so no mapping dict is needed. A first framing of this check flagged leichhardt/marrickville/parramatta as missing; that was a false alarm in the check itself -- those councils simply have no review-queue rows today, which is not a slug mismatch.
pre_impl.new_vs_existing: No new capability. dcp_commit_approved already ends with an enrichment block for fields inserted UNSET (v2_is_actionable, v2_topic, v2_applicable_dev_types); v2_precinct_id is the fourth field of that class and was left off the list. This extends that existing block rather than adding a parallel mechanism, and calls the existing derive_precinct_keys.run() rather than reimplementing keying.
pre_impl.external_source_error: The only external dependency is the production Postgres the derivation writes to. run() opens its own connection with connect_timeout=10 and sets statement_timeout=60s, and every call sits inside a per-council try/except here, so a database that is slow, down, or times out mid-pass degrades to a printed warning naming the exact re-run command. The provisions are already committed and live at that point, so the failure costs a keying pass, never a rollback. There is no HTTP call and no third-party API on this path.
pre_impl.frontend_type: No frontend change. The field this restores, v2_precinct_id, is consumed by the existing precinct serving code (frontend-nextjs precinct-service.ts and app/api/precinct/*), which reads it to match an address to provisions and already handles the NULL case by falling back to council-wide controls. That fallback is exactly why the bug was silent: the type at the boundary never changed, only the number of rows carrying a value, so nothing threw.
pre_impl.user_failure_mode: If this is too loose -- keys derived on the wrong rows -- a planning consultant is shown another precinct's controls as if they applied to their site, which is a confident wrong answer and the worst outcome. That risk is bounded by run()'s fingerprint gate, which fails closed and writes nothing when a PDF's pagination no longer matches the rule, and by --validate reproducing every existing hand-applied key before any write. If it is too tight -- keys not derived -- the symptom is the status quo this fixes and is visibly loggable: the run prints a warning naming the council and the command, and a precinct lookup serves council-wide controls rather than wrong ones. Loose fails silently, tight fails loudly, and the design is deliberately biased to the second.

functions.name: main
functions.input: argv (--commit or not). Internally: committed_councils, the set of councils that actually had provisions inserted this run, populated only after a per-chapter conn.commit() succeeds, so a rolled-back commit never adds its council.
functions.output: int return code, unchanged. New behaviour: after the three enrichment phases it calls derive_precinct_keys.run(council=<name>, apply=True, validate=False) once per committed council. Ordering is load-bearing -- a derived key also sets v2_dcp_layer='precinct' and run_layer_tagging writes the same column, so deriving first would have the layer overwritten and the row would stop matching the for-property route's precinct filter: key present, layer wrong, nothing served. The set deduplicates, so a council with several committed chapters is keyed once.
functions.if_none: An empty set (nothing committed, or every commit failed) skips the block entirely. A council with no RULES entry derives nothing and run() returns 0 rather than raising. If the module cannot even be imported -- derive_precinct_keys open()s data/cos_precinct_page_ranges.json at module scope, so a packaging slip raises FileNotFoundError, not ImportError -- the broad catch prints a warning naming that json and the loop is skipped, leaving the committed provisions live and unkeyed.

values.if_missing: validate=True would turn the pass into an assertion that derived keys reproduce EXISTING keys. Freshly committed rows have none, so it would fail on precisely the rows this exists to key. apply=False would derive and print the keys and write nothing.

break_it.scenario: The derivation is called in bulk instead of per council.
break_it.what_happens: run() hits its own footgun guard (`if apply and not council and not rule['validate']`) and SKIPS every validate:False rule, printing 'SKIPPED on bulk --apply'. Ashfield's 641 chapter-D rows stay unkeyed while the run reports success -- a silent half-fix that looks identical to a working one in the log summary.
break_it.how: The council name is threaded through from the commit loop, and test_the_derivation_is_scoped_to_a_named_council_never_bulk asserts it is never None or empty.
break_it.repro: Change council=council to council=None in the run() call; the scoping test goes red.

break_it.scenario: The data file data/cos_precinct_page_ranges.json is missing from the Railway image, so importing the derivation module raises before any council is keyed.
break_it.what_happens: derive_precinct_keys open()s it at module scope, so the IMPORT raises FileNotFoundError. That is not an ImportError, so a narrow handler lets it propagate out of main() AFTER the provisions are committed and live -- a crashed nightly job and a red monitor alert for a step that is re-runnable by hand.
break_it.how: Dockerfile.monitors now COPYs both the module and the json, the import is wrapped in `except Exception`, and the warning names the json so the next person does not have to rediscover the module-level read. test_a_missing_data_file_does_not_crash_an_already_committed_run and test_the_image_ships_the_json_the_derivation_reads_at_import pin both halves.
break_it.repro: Delete the json COPY line from Dockerfile.monitors, or narrow the catch to ImportError; either goes red.

break_it.scenario: The PDF was re-paginated, so a page_range rule's fingerprint no longer matches.
break_it.what_happens: run() FAILS CLOSED by design and writes no keys for that rule, rather than writing confident wrong-precinct keys. Rows serve council-wide plus precinct_warning, which is the safe failure.
break_it.how: Left as the script's behaviour deliberately -- this wiring does not override it. The per-council try/except turns the raise into a warning naming the exact command to re-run, so one council's fingerprint mismatch cannot stop the next council being keyed.
break_it.repro: test_a_derivation_error_does_not_fail_already_committed_provisions asserts both councils are still attempted and the fixing command is printed.

break_it.scenario: A human runs the worker without --commit to preview.
break_it.what_happens: The dry-run branch reports what it would commit and continues, so committed_councils stays empty and no keys are written.
break_it.how: Two independent guards: the empty set, and `not dry_run`. Mutation showed the second is currently redundant but becomes the only guard under a plausible refactor that records councils in the dry-run branch, so it is kept.

break_it.scenario: The rollback CSV is written inside an ephemeral container.
break_it.what_happens: run() writes data/db_rollback_backups/precinct_keying_derived_<date>.csv, which does not survive the Railway job. The backup is effectively local-only in production.
break_it.how: NOT mitigated, and deliberately out of scope. It is a real gap but a low-severity one here: precinct keys are DERIVED from a written rule, so the recovery path is re-running the derivation rather than replaying a CSV, and run() is idempotent. Recorded in residual_risk rather than fixed silently.
break_it.repro: Inspect the container filesystem after a dcp-commit run.

break_it.scenario: The derivation reports failure by RETURN VALUE rather than by raising, so the except block never fires.
break_it.what_happens: The commit job prints its ordinary success summary over a council whose keys were never written -- the same silent shape as the original bug.
break_it.how: Raised by cross-review on the pre-push run. Verified rather than accepted: run() returns 1 on exactly ONE path ('if validate and validation_failures'), which this call cannot reach because it passes validate=False -- so the scenario as described cannot fire today. The guard was added anyway because it costs nothing and stops the next non-zero path being silent, and the loop now `continue`s after the except so rc can never be read unbound or stale from the previous council. Probing it surfaced a worse case the review did NOT name: a page_range rule whose PDF has been re-paginated FAILS CLOSED, writes no keys, and returns 0 -- invisible from this side. That one is NOT fixed here and is recorded in residual_risk rather than implied to be covered.
break_it.repro: test_a_nonzero_return_is_reported_not_swallowed and test_a_zero_return_prints_no_warning; 4/4 mutants killed including dropping the `continue`.

mutation_analysis: Twelve reversions across three files, run as two harnesses. Wiring set (8): block deleted KILLED; council=None KILLED; apply=False KILLED; validate=True KILLED; dry_run guard dropped SURVIVED (redundant in current code -- a follow-up mutation proved it load-bearing under a refactor that records councils in the dry-run branch: guard present 9 passed, guard removed 1 failed, so it is kept rather than deleted); failed-commits-counted KILLED; try/except removed KILLED; warning loses the fixing command KILLED. Packaging/import set (4): narrow except ImportError KILLED; warning loses the json name KILLED (only after the test was FIXED -- mutation exposed it as weak, because the fake exception's own message contained the filename and was satisfying the assertion); json COPY removed KILLED; module COPY removed KILLED. Both harnesses assert the sources are restored byte-identical afterwards.
residual_risk: 0) THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST, and it is not fixed here: a page_range rule whose PDF has been re-paginated fails its fingerprint check, writes no keys, and returns 0. That fail-closed behaviour is correct -- council-wide beats confidently wrong-precinct -- but it is indistinguishable from success at the call site, so a council can go unkeyed with a clean log. Catching it needs a coverage assertion over the corpus (every served provision in a keyed council has a key), which is what scripts/audit_precinct_keying_coverage.py is for and it is wired to nothing. 1) NINE precinct labels that had rows before still serve nothing, because no derivation rule covers them: leichhardt PART_G_OVERVIEW (414 rows), waverley E7 (111), and seven Ashfield named precincts -- Ashfield Town Centre (101), Hurlstone Park (100), Ashfield South (66), Croydon South (65), Canterbury Road (46), Ashfield East (44), Summer Hill (33). This PR wires up the derivation; it does not write new rules, so those stay unkeyed until someone writes them. Registered here rather than left implicit. 2) The rollback CSV does not persist in the container (see break_it). 3) The wiring runs on the dcp-commit path only. A council whose provisions arrive by any other route -- a manual backfill, a direct insert -- still needs the derivation run by hand; nothing yet asserts corpus-wide that a served provision in a keyed council has a key, which is the check that would make this class of bug impossible rather than merely fixed. scripts/audit_precinct_keying_coverage.py exists and is not wired to anything either. The new real-layer test narrows this: it catches rule/data DRIFT (a rule that no longer reproduces production keys) and slug drift, but it does NOT assert that every served provision in a keyed council has a key -- that corpus-wide check is still unwritten, and is what would make this class of bug impossible rather than merely fixed.

post_merge.db_reset: None. This PR changes no data. The production keys were already restored during the session that found the bug (1,560 updates, rollback CSVs at data/db_rollback_backups/precinct_keying_derived_2026-09-10.csv).
post_merge.secrets: None added. The derivation reads DATABASE_URL, which the dcp-commit Railway service already sets.
post_merge.manual_verify: After the next dcp-commit run, confirm the log contains 'Re-deriving precinct keys for N committed council(s)' and that no '[warn] could not load the precinct derivation' line appears -- that line would mean the Railway image did not pick up the two new COPY lines. Then re-check keyed counts for the councils named in that run.
